t.1.100.1: Then, at the proper time, when her daughter-in-law had bathed after her season, Satyavatī, leading her to the bed, softly spoke these words.
t.1.100.3: Having heard those words of her mother-in-law, she, lying on a beautiful bed, then thought of Bhīṣma and the other bulls among the Kurus.
t.1.100.2: Kausalyā, you have a brother-in-law; today he will come in to you. Wait for him vigilantly in the coming night.
t.1.100.4: Then the truthful seer, appointed first to Ambikā, entered her bedchamber while the lamps were burning brightly.
t.1.100.5: Seeing the tawny matted locks of that Kṛṣṇa, his blazing eyes, and his reddish-brown beard, the queen shut her eyes.
t.1.100.6: Wishing to do what was pleasing to his mother, he united with her in the night; but the daughter of Kāśi, out of fear, could not bear to look at him.
t.1.100.7: Then, approaching her son as he came out, the mother said to him: "Son, will a virtuous prince be born in her?"
t.1.100.8: Having heard those words of his mother, Vyāsa, supremely wise, whose knowledge transcended the senses, spoke, impelled by destiny.
t.1.100.10: And he too will have a hundred sons of great strength; but because of his mother's fault, he himself will be born blind.
t.1.100.9: He will have the strength of ten thousand elephants; he will be learned, the best of royal seers, greatly fortunate, of great valour and of great intelligence.
t.1.100.12: You ought to give a protector of the lineage of our kin, one who will increase the line of the ancestors, a second king of the Kuru line.
t.1.100.11: Having heard those words of his, the mother then said to her son: “A blind man is not a fitting king for the Kurus, O you whose wealth is austerity.”
t.1.100.13: Having promised, "So be it," the great ascetic departed; and Kausalyā, in due time, gave birth to that son of hers, who was blind.
t.1.100.15: Then, by that same rite, the great seer approached her; he came to Ambālikā, and she too, on seeing the seer, became dejected and turned pale, O Bhārata.
t.1.100.14: Then once again that blameless queen Satyā, having spoken to her daughter-in-law and instructed her, summoned the seer as before.
t.1.100.16: Seeing her frightened, pale, and despondent, O king, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, spoke these words.
t.1.100.18: "And that very thing shall be his name here, O fair-faced lady." Having spoken thus, the blessed lord, the best of seers, departed.
t.1.100.17: Because you turned pale on seeing me, misshapen as I am, this son of yours shall be pale indeed, and Pāṇḍu shall be his name.
t.1.100.20: His mother asked him once again for one more son, and the great seer replied to his mother, "So be it."
t.1.100.19: Then, seeing her son come out, Satyā spoke to him, and he in turn told his mother of that child's paleness.
t.1.100.21: Then, when her time had come, that queen gave birth to a son, Pāṇḍu, endowed with auspicious marks and seeming to blaze with splendor. To him were born five sons, the Pāṇḍavas, great archers.
t.1.100.23: Then the daughter of the lord of Kāśi adorned a slave-girl, who was like an Apsaras, with her own ornaments, and sent her to Kṛṣṇa.
t.1.100.24: The slave woman rose to meet the seer when he arrived and greeted him respectfully; then, permitted by him, she lay down with him, and, having honoured him, she attended upon him.
t.1.100.22: Then, at the time of her season, she again assigned the elder daughter-in-law to him; but she, who was like a daughter of the gods, recalling the great seer's form and that smell, did not do the queen's bidding, out of fear.
t.1.100.25: Through the enjoyment of love the seer found satisfaction in her; the great seer stayed the night with her, who was delighted.
t.1.100.26: Rising, he said to her, "You will no longer be a slave. And this glorious embryo that has come into your womb, O lovely one, will be righteous-souled in the world, the foremost of all the wise."
t.1.100.27: He was born as the one named Vidura, the son of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, the brother of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and of Pāṇḍu, a man of boundless intelligence.
t.1.100.28: Through the curse of that great-souled Māṇḍavya, Dharma was born in the form of Vidura, a knower of the true nature of things, free from desire and anger.
t.1.100.30: Thus, in the field of Vicitravīrya, and from Dvaipāyana, were born sons resembling the offspring of gods, who would increase the lineage of the Kurus.
t.1.100.29: Having thus become free of his debt to Dharma, he met once more with his mother, and after making known to her the conception, he vanished right there.
